state.misconception_label: Does not realise that adding a larger number gives a larger answer

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Tom and Katie are discussing related calculations Tom says if you know that \( 3748+426=4174 \), then \( 3748+427 \) must equal \( \mathbf{4 1 7 5} \) Katie says if you know that \( 3748-426=3322 \), then \( 3748 \) - \( 427 \) must equal \( \mathbf{3 3 2 3} \) Who is correct? I got Only Katie because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of adding numbers like adding ingredients in a recipe. Just like adding more flour makes a bigger batch of cookies, adding a larger number will give you a larger total. So, in this case, when you add 426 to 3748, you get 4174. What would happen if you added one more to 426?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if I add one more to 426, that makes it 427, which is bigger... so the answer should be bigger too? So 3748 + 427 would be 4175, not 4174? But then why did I think Katie was right about the subtraction one?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of dividing numbers like sharing a pizza. Just like dividing the pizza into smaller slices gives you more pieces, dividing by a smaller number will give you a larger answer. So, in this case, when you subtract 427 from 3748, you get 3321. What would happen if you subtracted one less than 427?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the addition misconception with an appropriate analogy, but makes a critical mathematical error in Turn 3 by incorrectly analogizing division to subtraction and providing wrong information about the relationship, which undermines the overall quality despite the student showing some progress on the addition concept.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use real-world analogies (recipe ingredients, pizza slices), the analogies are poorly matched to the mathematical operations—the pizza division analogy in Turn 3 confuses division with subtraction and provides incorrect mathematical reasoning, undermining the experiential approach.
